caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 75 of 1984 with Civil Rule No. 205 (fm) of 1984.
lawyer:
Fakir Shahabuddin, Abdur Rab 1 and Abdul Halim, Advocates ------ For the Appellant. 
Mohammadullah, Advocate ------ For Respondent No.2
 Nurul Islam, Advocate ------For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Bengal Ceramic Industries Ltd  ------ Applicant
Vs.
Chairman, Petro Bangla & others   ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration that the action of the defendants in disconnecting gas line of the plaintiff and continuance of such disconnection from 28-12-83 are all illegal, arbitrary, malafide, void and without jurisdiction, and for injunction directing the defendants to reconnect and restore gas line and connection of gas to the factory premises of the plaintiff and for compensation of Taka 91,40,000 and such other reliefs. According to the plaintiff, after due compliance of the requirements and formalities and on payment of security deposit for obtaining the gas line and connection in the factory premises an agreement dated 19.4.77 was entered into between the plaintiff and defendant No.2. In terms of the said agreement the defendants had been supplying gas to the plaintiffs factory which had been using and operating 20 burners till 27-11-83 and from 28- 12-83 the said connection was disconnected upon the plea of non-deposit of security money. Defendant No.2 by a letter dated 5-9-83 asked the plaintiff to deposit Taka 2,02,690 out of which Taka 65,830 in cash/pay order/bank draft, and Taka 1,36,860 by Protirokha Sonchoy Potro. This demand and mode of payment were contrary to the agreement dated 19-4-77; Defendant No. 2 by another letter dated 8-11-83 again demanded the said amount threatening disconnection of gas. The plaintiff by a letter dated 15-11-83 apprised defendant No.2 that the matter was pending before the Minister-in-Charge of Industries for consideration. Defendant No.2, however, disconnected the plaintiffs gas line on 28-12-83. The plaintiff, in the meantime, made deposit of Taka 2,02,680 in accordance with the terms of the agreement dated 19-4-77 and furnished the same on 9-1-84. But in spite of the compliance of the demand of deposit of additional security deposit defendant No.2 did not restore the gas connection to the factory premises of the plaintiff. The plaintiff is entitled to the legal right to use gas in its factory premises in terms of the contract, and the actions of the defendant No.2 are not warranted by law. In the aforesaid circumstances, an application was made for temporary injunction in mandatory form. 

 3. Defendant No. 2 appeared by filing a written objection and denying the material allegations made in the application for injunction, contended that the Government in exercise of the statutory powers refixed the rate of gas for industrial category with effect from 2-6-79 as per Government Notification. Defendant No.2 further stated that the increase in the security deposit and the monthly minimum charges were communicated by the letter dated 9-9-79 and the tariff enhancing the charges was made effective from 2-6-79. The defendant No.2 also asserted that the plaintiff defaulted in making payment of revised security deposit from time to time. The defendant No.2 legally asked the plaintiff by the letter dated 5-9-83 to deposit Taka 2,02,690 out of which Taka 65,830 in the form of cash/pay order/bank draft and Taka 1,36,860 in the form of Protirokha Sonchoy Potro as the mode of payment of security deposit has been revised by the Board of Directors of the defendant Company in its meeting dated 13-3-80. The plaintiff was repeatedly asked to deposit the balance security money and the plaintiff failed to do so which resulted to disconnection of the gas line on 28-12-83. Defendant No.2 further stated that the plaintiff was also a defaulter in payment of gas bills and. an amount of Taka 2,72,413/15 was outstanding to the Government, Certain other pleas in bar to the suit were also raised opposing the prayer for temporary injunction. 

 4. The learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer for temporary injunction, mainly, on the ground that "the gas line of the plaintiff was disconnected on 28-12-83 i.e. 25 days before the filing of the suit" and according to the learned Subordinate Judge mandatory injunction could not be granted to establish a new state of fact different from those existing on the date of institution of the suit. According to the trial Court, the plaintiff did not come with clean hands, and therefore, balance of convenience and inconvenience was not in favour of the plaintiff. 

 5. Mr Fakir Shahabuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal, contends that there is no dispute on the fact that the plaintiff is a consumer of gas for industrial purposes. There is also no dispute that after due compliance of the requirements and formalities. gas connection was made to the plaintiffs factory under a contract dated 19-4-77. It is also evident that certain changes were made in the meantime in the tariff. The plaintiff was asked by defendant No.2 to put in some money as security deposit. The plaintiff made the deposit but not in the way suggested by defendant No.2. The plaintiff made the security deposit amounting to Taka 2,02,690 on 9-1-84. It is apparent that the plaintiff did not make the deposit according to the direction given in the letter dated 5- 9-83 of defendant No.2. Thus the apparent dispute between the parties seems to rest on the mode of payment. Subject to the disposal of the suit on merits at the trial where all the questions will be gone into threadbare, it appears that the plaintiff has put in Taka 2,02,690. The plaintiff paid an amount of Taka 25,000 in the form of pay order and the balance of Taka 1,77,690 in the form of Bank guarantee and not in the form of Protirokha Sonchoy Potro. It does not make any difference in payment, since the bank guarantee is also a recognised mode of payment. To us it seems that there is no law by which a party to a contract may insist that payment should be made according to its dictates. There is no dispute that pay order, bank draft and cash are recognised forms of payment. There is also no dispute that bank guarantee is also a recognised mode of payment and ensures payment of money when demanded. There is no reason to hold that a party should be directed to make payment in terms of Protirokha Sonchoy Potro. The learned Advocate for the respondents could not satisfy us that there is any legal background in favour of such demand regulating the mode of payments. 

 6. We do not intend to express opinion on other questions at this stage. In the interest of a fair and complete justice to the parties, it is sufficient to observe that the plaintiff at this stage is not required to prove the case on merits. The disclosures made by the plaintiff and supported by the papers produced by it, indicate a prima facie case for injunction in favour of the plaintiff. Evidently, the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff. It may not be lost sight of that the plaintiff is an industrial concern, and gas is an indispensable energy for running the industry in a developing country like Bangladesh. We have noticed that the plaintiffs unit was earlier operated by electricity. It had to convert the system from electricity to gas. The decision in the case of Abdul Barek Mia and others vs ABM Serajul Islam (20 DLR 508) does not help the respondents in the least. In this case it has been held that the Court has inherent power to pass an order of mandatory injunction even under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case, the learned Subordinate Judge proceeded to dispose of the temporary injunction matter on hearing the parties. Mr Mohammadullah, learned Advocate appearing for respondents No.2, has also drawn our attention to two other decisions of this Court. The case of Abdul Jalil Munshi vs Abu Bakar Siddique, 35 DLR (AD) 42 does not help Mr Mohammadullah in the facts of the instant case. In this case, the scope of injunction has been examined from different perspectives relying on the facts and circumstances of each case. Nothing has been shown that mandatory injunction in the nature prayed for is not available. On the other hand, it appears from the aforesaid decision that mandatory injunction on an interlocutory application may be granted to restore status quo. Mr Mohammadullah, however, emphasised on status quo existing on the date of institution of the suit. Evidently, gas connection was cut off on 28-12-83, and the suit was filed about 25 days thereafter. But in the facts of the instant case, the status quo of the plaintiff as to its status as a consumer of gas for industrial purpose goes back to 19-4-77, and it was continuing to enjoy the said status till it was disconnected. The proper remedy for mandatory injunction in terms of section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, seems to be attracted in the facts of the instant case. The decision in the case of Jupiter Glass Industries Ltd and others vs Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited and another, 35 DLR 293 is distinguishable on facts. In that case temporary injunction was refused on a different ground. Immediate inconvenience of the plaintiff was not remedied by an injunction because of certain changes in tariff. In the facts of the instant case, the plaintiff has already deposited the enhanced demand on the strength of changed tariff. Therefore, the plaintiff seems to be entitled to the equitable relief of injunction. 

 7. The case of Nandan Pictures Ltd vs Art Pictures Ltd. and others AIR 1956 Cal 428 does not help defendants for simple proposition that "Injunctions are a form of equitable relief and they have to be adjusted in aid of equity and justice to the facts of each particular case." New set of equity as raised by Mr Mohammadullah is not based on objectivity. Equity was that the plaintiff was entitled to the use of gas according to its status as the consumer of gas. It's status as such was disturbed by the impugned action, and remedy was sought by way of temporary mandatory injunction. It is for the period of the suit and the Court has ample jurisdiction to grant such relief in the interest of adjustment of equity in aid of justice. We are not oblivious that suspension of production of an industrial unit like the plaintiff may cause injury to the developments proceeding in the industrial world. We would however, direct the learned Subordinate Judge to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible. The defendants are directed to put in their written statements within two weeks from date, and the parties should be given lawful opportunities to represent their respective cases. Without prejudice to the right of defendant No. 2 at the trial, defendant No. 2 is directed to restore gas connection to the plaintiffs factory forthwith. In the event of any shortfall in the deposit, the matter may be adjusted at the trial of the suit. The learned Subordinate Judge is accordingly, directed to dispose of the suit within 30th September, 1984.
